The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and directly serves its emotional themes. The first half of the story stretches out a single afternoon in late May, lingering on sensory details, small domestic chores, and the specific rhythms of the mother-son dialogue. This unhurried pacing allows the reader to fully absorb the mother's fierce independence, her quirks, and the deep, quiet affection between the two characters. 

Following the scene break, the writer effectively uses time compression, summarizing an entire month into a single three-sentence paragraph before jumping straight into the crisis in late June. This sudden acceleration mirrors the jarring nature of the phone call and the abrupt onset of age-related emergencies. Finally, the story slows down (stretches) once more at the very end as Paul stands in front of the open refrigerator. Drawing out this brief, quiet moment allows the poignant realization of his mother's solitude and fragility—crystallized by the untouched, month-old meatloaf and the labeled receipt—to fully land with the reader.
